stem: A student keeps her right hand in warm water for two minutes and then dips it in tap water. How will the tap water most likely feel to that hand?
options: It will feel warm
It will feel cool
It will feel boiling hot
It will feel ice-cold and painful
explanation: Correct option: (B). The hand has just come from warm water, so the tap water, which is less hot than the warm water, feels cool to it. It will not feel warm, since it is colder than what the hand was in; it is neither boiling hot nor ice-cold, because tap water is only at an ordinary temperature.

stem: In Activity 7.1, the same tap water felt cool to one hand and warm to the other. What do we learn from this?
options: Touch cannot always tell correctly how hot a body is
Tap water is always warmer than water from a matka
The right hand is always warmer than the left hand
Water changes its temperature when a hand touches it
explanation: Correct option: (A). Both hands touched the same water at the same time, yet they felt it differently, so our sense of touch is not a reliable judge of hotness. The activity says nothing about matka water, the two hands are not always at different temperatures, and the water did not change; only the feeling did.

stem: Phiban touched Lambok's forehead and felt he might have a fever, but she still measured his temperature. Why was measuring the better choice?
options: A thermometer also brings down a mild fever
Doctors never allow anyone to touch the forehead
Touch can mislead, but a thermometer is reliable
A forehead is always colder than the rest of the body
explanation: Correct option: (C). Whether a forehead feels hot depends on how warm the toucher's own hand is, so touch can give a wrong idea; a thermometer gives a reliable value. stem: Rani comes in after playing in snow and says a glass of water feels warm. Her brother comes in from a hot, sunny verandah and says the same water feels cool. Which explanation is best?
options: The water changes temperature when each person touches it
Rani's hand was warmer than her brother's hand
The water is warm in one part and cool in another
Each judges it against how hot or cold their own hand was
explanation: Correct option: (D). Rani's hand was very cold from the snow, so the water feels warm to her; her brother's hand was hot, so the same water feels cool to him. stem: Two pots of water look the same. Which method gives the most reliable answer to which pot is hotter?
options: Dip one hand in the first pot and then the same hand in the second
Measure the temperature of each pot with the same thermometer
Ask two friends to touch one pot each and say which is hotter

stem: Water in jug X is at 45 °C and water in jug Y is at 30 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: Y is hotter than X by 15 °C
X is hotter than Y by 15 °C
X is hotter than Y by 75 °C
X and Y are equally hot
explanation: Correct option: (B). A hotter body has a higher temperature, and the difference tells how much hotter it is: 45 °C - 30 °C = 15 °C, so X is hotter by 15 °C. Y has the lower temperature, so it is colder; 75 °C comes from wrongly adding the two temperatures; and different temperatures mean they are not equally hot.

stem: A digital thermometer placed in a small child's armpit reads 36.4 °C. What is the child's actual body temperature likely to be?
options: Exactly 36.4 °C
About 35.4 °C to 35.9 °C
About 36.9 °C to 37.4 °C
About 38.4 °C to 39.4 °C
explanation: Correct option: (C). A reading in the armpit is about 0.5 °C to 1 °C lower than the actual body temperature, so add these: 36.4 + 0.5 = 36.9 °C and 36.4 + 1 = 37.4 °C. Taking the reading as exact ignores this difference, 35.4-35.9 °C subtracts instead of adding, and 38.4-39.4 °C adds far too much.

stem: A healthy student's temperature reads 36.8 °C. Her friend says she must be unwell because it is not 37.0 °C. Which judgement is correct?
options: Yes; any value other than 37.0 °C shows that a person is unwell
Yes; a reading below 37.0 °C means the thermometer is faulty
No; every healthy person's temperature is fixed at 36.8 °C
No; 37.0 °C is an average, so small differences are normal
explanation: Correct option: (D). Normal temperature is the average body temperature of a large number of healthy people, so a healthy person may have a temperature slightly different from 37.0 °C; it also changes with age, time of day and activity. So 36.8 °C is not a sign of illness or of a faulty thermometer, and body temperature is not fixed at any single value for everyone.

stem: Komal says she has a fever of 101 degrees. On which scale is she most likely giving her temperature, and why?

Celsius, as clinical thermometers mostly use the Celsius scale

stem: On a thermometer, there are 20 small divisions between the 20 °C and 30 °C marks. The top of the liquid column is 5 small divisions above the 20 °C mark. What is the reading?
explanation: Correct option: (A). One small division = (30 - 20) °C / 20 = 0.5 °C. Five divisions above 20 °C is 5 x 0.5 = 2.5 °C, so the reading is 20 + 2.5 = 22.5 °C. 25.0 °C takes each division as 1 °C, 20.5 °C takes each as 0.1 °C, and 21.0 °C takes each as 0.2 °C.

stem: A thermometer in crushed ice reads 0 °C. Five minutes later, while plenty of ice is still melting, it is read again. What is expected, and why?

The same reading, as melting ice keeps a constant temperature

stem: Maximum and minimum air temperatures of a town were: Day 1: 33 °C and 19 °C; Day 2: 36 °C and 25 °C; Day 3: 30 °C and 24 °C; Day 4: 31 °C and 18 °C. On which day was the difference between the maximum and minimum temperatures the greatest?

Day 3
Day 4
